summary: Jay Alammar's visual walkthrough of the Transformer from 'Attention Is All You Need': stacks of six encoders and decoders, where each word's embedding is projected to query, key and value vectors and self-attention mixes information across positions. It builds up multi-head attention (8 heads of 64-d Q/K/V from 512-d embeddings), sinusoidal positional encodings, residual + layer-norm sublayers, masked decoder self-attention and the final linear + softmax over the vocabulary.
takeaways: Self-attention for one token = softmax(q·k_j / √d_k) weights over all positions, used to average the value vectors; in matrix form it is a few matmuls, which is why it parallelises where an RNN cannot.
Multi-head attention runs 8 independent Q/K/V projections, concatenates the outputs and mixes them with W_O — letting different heads attend to different positions and representation subspaces.

Attention is order-agnostic, so position must be injected (sinusoidal encodings added to the embeddings); the decoder additionally masks future positions with −∞ before the softmax and uses encoder–decoder attention with queries from the decoder and keys/values from the encoder.
relevance: Transformers are the backbone of the masked-diffusion and single-cell foundation models you build on (e.g. scGPT/Geneformer-style encoders), and the attention-as-weighted-average view is the natural way to let isoforms of the same gene share information in an scIso-style predictor. Having the mechanics crisp also pays off directly for supervising the deep learning course, where tomorrow's chapter is transformers.
brief: Focus on the self-attention section (the Q/K/V and score → softmax → weighted sum steps) and the matrix form; the training/decoding part at the end can be skimmed. It pairs naturally with today's Goodfellow Ch. 10 reading — RNNs pass information through a sequential hidden state with O(τ) unparallelisable steps, attention replaces that with direct all-to-all mixing. Question to keep in mind: what does the √d_k scaling protect against, and what would go wrong in the softmax without it?

extras.summary: Normalizing flows build a density by pushing a standard normal through an invertible network and scoring data with the change-of-variables formula (Eq. 16.3): base log-density at f⁻¹(x) minus the log absolute Jacobian determinant. The chapter is mostly about which layers make that tractable — linear (LU-parameterised), elementwise, coupling, autoregressive and residual (iRevNet, iResNet) flows — then multi-scale flows, GLOW and fitting a flow to a target density via reverse KL.
takeaways: The density goes down where the map stretches space and up where it compresses it; the |det Jacobian| term is exactly that volume correction, and training is plain maximum likelihood (Eq. 16.8).

Every layer must be invertible, cheap to invert and have a cheap Jacobian determinant; coupling flows get a triangular Jacobian by transforming half the variables conditioned on the other half, with permutations between layers so everything mixes.

Flows are the only model in the book with exact likelihoods, but the latent must have the same dimension as the data, and sampling quality lagged GANs and diffusion — which is the motivation for continuous-time flows and flow matching.
pitfalls: Why the inverse of the Jacobian determinant appears: use the 1D picture (Fig. 16.2) — probability mass in an interval is conserved, so if the interval gets twice as wide the density must halve.

Masked autoregressive vs inverse autoregressive flows: one is fast to evaluate likelihoods (training) and slow to sample, the other the reverse — a 2×2 table of 'which direction is parallel' clears it up.
The conditioner network in a coupling layer need not be invertible — only g must be; students often think the whole network has to be bijective.
extras.links: This is the discrete-layer ancestor of the continuous flows in Lipman's flow matching and the generator matching guide you have read: replace the stack of layers with an ODE and the log-det sum becomes the integrated divergence (and Hutchinson's trace estimator, Eq. 16.24, shows up again in FFJORD-style likelihoods).

extras.summary: Prince builds the VAE from the nonlinear latent variable model Pr(x)=∫Norm[f(z),σ²I]Norm[z;0,I]dz: the marginal likelihood is intractable, so Jensen's inequality gives the ELBO, which is tight when q equals the posterior. An amortised Gaussian encoder approximates that posterior, the ELBO is estimated with one Monte Carlo sample plus a closed-form KL, and the reparameterisation trick makes it differentiable; the chapter ends with importance-sampled likelihoods, generation, resynthesis and disentanglement.
takeaways: The VAE is a training device for a latent variable model, not the model itself; the model is just prior + decoder.
The ELBO can be read three ways — Jensen bound, log-likelihood minus KL(q‖posterior), and reconstruction minus KL(q‖prior) — and the gap is exactly the KL to the true posterior (Fig. 17.6).
Reparameterisation (z = μ + Σ^{1/2}ε) moves the randomness to an input branch so gradients reach the encoder; better likelihood estimates come from importance sampling with the encoder as proposal.
pitfalls: 'Reconstruction loss' with a Gaussian decoder is MSE only up to σ²; with σ fixed, students don't see that the reconstruction–KL trade-off depends on it — show how scaling σ reweights the two terms.
Why vanilla VAE samples are blurry: the decoder mean is shown and the spherical Gaussian noise is dropped (Fig. 17.12); the noise model, not the network, is the bottleneck.
Prior vs aggregated posterior: sampling from N(0,I) can land in latent regions the encoder never uses — point to the aggregated-posterior trick and to hierarchical/learned priors.
extras.links: Familiar ground from scVI, which swaps the Gaussian decoder for a negative binomial one — the same move as your NB + multinomial isoform model; the importance-sampling estimator in 17.8.1 is the one-sample-to-K-sample step that IWAE (on your path) turns into a tighter bound.

extras.summary: Chapter 12 builds the transformer from dot-product self-attention: each output is a softmax-weighted routing of shared value vectors, with weights from query–key similarity, extended by positional encodings, √D_q scaling and multiple heads, then wrapped in residual + LayerNorm + per-token MLP layers. It then walks through encoders (BERT, masked-token pre-training then fine-tuning), decoders (GPT3, masked self-attention for autoregressive next-token prediction), encoder–decoders with cross-attention, sparse attention for long sequences, and ViT/SWin for images.
takeaways: Self-attention = shared linear maps for values/queries/keys plus data-dependent mixing weights (Eq. 12.5–12.9): parameter count is independent of sequence length N, but compute is quadratic in N; without positional encodings it is permutation-equivariant.

Encoder vs decoder is a training-objective and masking choice: BERT predicts randomly masked tokens using both contexts; GPT sets future dot products to −∞ so every position contributes a next-token loss in one forward pass (Eq. 12.15).
Inductive bias trades against data: ViT has to learn the 2D structure CNNs get for free and only beat contemporary CNNs with very large pre-training sets.
pitfalls: Shapes in the matrix form (X is D×N, softmax over columns of KᵀQ) — have students write the dimensions of every term in Eq. 12.8 before coding; the book's column convention differs from PyTorch's row convention.
Why √D_q? Large dot products saturate the softmax and kill gradients; a quick numerical demo with random vectors of growing dimension makes it concrete.
Causal masking confusion: the mask is applied to the logits (−∞ before softmax), not to the attention weights afterwards, and it is what lets training be parallel while generation stays sequential.
extras.links: BERT's masked-token objective is the one-step ancestor of the masked diffusion models (MDLM/MD4) on your path, and this chapter is the textbook companion to the Illustrated Transformer you have open.

extras.summary: Chapter 13 represents a graph by an adjacency matrix A, node embeddings X and edge embeddings E, and demands that every layer be equivariant to node permutations (H P = F[H P, PᵀAP]). It builds a simple GCN layer that sums neighbours via H(A+I), covers graph-, node- and edge-level tasks, inductive vs transductive settings with neighbourhood sampling and graph partitioning for huge graphs, and variants of aggregation (mean, Kipf normalisation, max, graph attention) plus edge graphs.
takeaways: A GCN layer is convolution with a relational inductive bias: shared parameters at every node and messages aggregated from neighbours, H_{k+1} = a[β1ᵀ + Ω H_k (A+I)] (Eq. 13.10).
Node and edge outputs must be permutation-equivariant; graph-level outputs become invariant via pooling such as the mean H_K 1/N (Eq. 13.7).
Graph attention is self-attention masked to A+I (Eq. 13.24): the transformer is a GNN on a fully connected graph, and a GAT is attention restricted to the graph's edges.
pitfalls: Equivariance vs invariance for graphs — use the toxic-molecule (invariant) vs per-atom label (equivariant) examples and verify Eq. 13.6 on a 3-node graph.
Transductive training on one big graph feels like 'cheating' to students — explain that only labelled nodes enter the loss, while unlabelled nodes still pass messages.
Sum vs mean vs Kipf normalisation — sum keeps degree information (structure), mean removes it; Kipf's D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2} down-weights hub nodes. A star graph shows the difference immediately.
extras.links: This is the entry point to your GRL track (Hamilton's book) and the E(n)-equivariant GNNs behind protein SE(3) generation; the 'transformer = GNN on a complete graph' view also links today's two chapters to the Transformers are Graph Neural Networks paper on your path.

extras.summary: Sections 10.1–10.3 introduce RNNs via unfolding a recurrence h(t)=f(h(t−1),x(t);θ) into a computational graph with shared parameters, so one transition function handles any sequence length. They cover the standard hidden-to-hidden RNN (Eq. 10.8–10.14) and its training by back-propagation through time, output-recurrent networks trained with teacher forcing, RNNs as directed graphical models over y, conditioning on a context vector, and bidirectional RNNs.
takeaways: Parameter sharing across time is the core idea: unfolding turns the recurrent circuit into a deep feedforward graph, and BPTT is just ordinary backprop on that graph — with O(τ) time and memory that cannot be parallelised over steps.

Teacher forcing follows from maximum likelihood: condition step t+1 on the true y(t); it decouples time steps for output-recurrent nets, but creates a train/test mismatch when the model later runs free on its own outputs (mitigated by mixing in generated inputs, scheduled-sampling style).

As a probabilistic model an RNN parametrises a fully connected directed graphical model over the sequence with O(1) parameters in τ, because the hidden state h(t) summarises the whole past; bidirectional RNNs add a backward-in-time state so o(t) can depend on past and future.
pitfalls: 'Unfolded graph' vs 'circuit diagram' confuses students — draw both for three steps and point out that W, U, V appear once in the circuit but at every step in the unfolded graph.
Why can't BPTT be parallelised? Show that h(t) needs h(t−1); contrast with an output-recurrent net under teacher forcing where every step's input is known from the data.
Exposure bias from teacher forcing — explain with a toy autoregressive sampler that drifts off the training distribution after one wrong prediction.
extras.links: The autoregressive factorisation and the teacher-forcing train/test gap are the same issues that motivate masked diffusion and discrete flow matching, which generate all positions in parallel and train on corrupted rather than ground-truth contexts.

extras.summary: Sections 10.4–10.12 cover encoder–decoder (seq2seq) RNNs and their fixed-size context bottleneck, deep and recursive RNNs, and the central difficulty of long-term dependencies: repeated multiplication by the same Jacobian makes gradients vanish or explode with its spectral radius. The rest surveys remedies — echo state networks, skip connections and leaky units, gated units (LSTM, GRU), gradient norm clipping, and explicit memory with soft attention-style addressing.
takeaways: Vanishing/exploding gradients come from powers of the recurrent Jacobian: eigenvalues with |λ|<1 shrink as λ^t and |λ|>1 blow up, so long-range signals are exponentially weaker than short-range ones (10.7).

Gated RNNs (LSTM, GRU) create paths through time whose derivative stays near 1 — a linear self-loop on the cell state whose weight is a learned, input-dependent forget gate — generalising fixed-time-constant leaky units.
Gradient norm clipping handles 'cliffs' in the loss landscape by rescaling large gradients while keeping their direction; it fixes explosion but not vanishing, which needs architectural changes.
pitfalls: Students often think LSTMs 'remove' vanishing gradients entirely — explain that they add an additive memory path whose gradient is a product of forget-gate values, which the network can keep near 1 when it needs to.
Clipping by value vs by norm: norm clipping preserves the update direction; per-minibatch clipping is biased relative to the true gradient.
The seq2seq bottleneck — a single context vector for the whole input — is the natural bridge to attention (Bahdanau et al.), which the chapter mentions in 10.12 and the transformer chapter builds on.
extras.links: The spectral-radius argument is the same one behind initialisation (UDL Ch. 7, read yesterday) and reappears for any iterated map, including long CTMC/ODE sampling chains; leaky units and gating are the conceptual ancestors of residual streams in the transformers your models use.

extras.summary: A short chapter framing unsupervised learning: models learned from unlabelled data, of which generative models map latent variables to data and probabilistic ones (flows, VAEs, diffusion) also assign a likelihood, while GANs only sample. It lists desirable properties of generative models — efficient, high-quality sampling, coverage, well-behaved and disentangled latent spaces, efficient likelihood — and introduces evaluation by test likelihood, Inception score, FID and manifold precision/recall.
takeaways: No single generative model family has all desirable properties (Fig. 14.3): GANs sample well but have no likelihood; flows give exact likelihoods; VAEs and diffusion only give bounds.
Evaluate likelihood on held-out data, never on training data — a model can memorise training points and still have terrible coverage.

IS, FID and precision/recall measure different things: IS rewards confident, class-balanced samples; FID compares Gaussian fits in Inception feature space; precision (realism) and recall (coverage) separate the two failure modes using k-NN hyperspheres.
pitfalls: Students conflate 'generative' with 'probabilistic' — point out GANs generate but assign no probability, and autoregressive transformers are probabilistic without latent variables.
FID is often treated as ground truth — stress that it depends entirely on the feature extractor and its Gaussian approximation, and isn't meaningful outside natural images.
Precision vs recall intuition: mode collapse = high precision, low recall; blurry over-dispersed samples = high recall, low precision.
extras.links: For your single-cell and isoform models the image metrics don't transfer — the precision/recall idea (in a sensible feature space, or on held-out likelihood for the NB + multinomial model) is the one worth carrying over, and it sets up Friday's flows and VAE chapters.

summary: A short Nature review arguing that alternative splicing is the main way ~20,000 human genes produce a far larger proteome: sequencing suggests 95–100% of multi-exon human pre-mRNAs are alternatively processed, with anywhere from two to thousands of isoforms per gene. It walks through the four basic splicing modules, how a small set of mostly ubiquitous regulators (SR proteins, hnRNPs, a few tissue-specific factors) control >100,000 decisions, the kinetic coupling of splicing to transcription elongation and chromatin, and closes on the open question of how much of this diversity is functional.
takeaways: Almost all alternative splicing is built from four modules — alternative 5′ site, alternative 3′ site, cassette exon, retained intron — combined to give e.g. >500 KCNMA1 isoforms or 38,016 possible Dscam isoforms.

Regulation is combinatorial and kinetic: SR-protein enhancers vs hnRNP silencers (the 'yin-yang' model), with outcomes also shaped by competing splice sites, Pol II elongation rate and marks like H3K36me3.
Whether most isoforms are functional or tolerated noise was unresolved in 2010, and the authors say so plainly.
keyFigure: Fig. 2: generation of diverse mRNA repertoires — KCNMA1 (>500 isoforms from combined alternative exons and splice sites), Dscam's four clusters of mutually exclusive exons, and trans-splicing in mod(mdg4).
relevance: This is the biology behind your state space: each gene's isoforms are combinations of these modules, so isoform counts with a fixed gene total live on a lattice simplex whose dimension ranges from 2 to thousands. The point that a few dozen regulators (themselves expressed genes) drive most splicing decisions is also the biological case for scIso — predicting isoform usage from gene expression.
brief: Read the first two sections and the 'Mechanisms' part carefully (Figs. 1–3); the bioinformatics and evolution sections can be skimmed. It builds directly on Kelemen et al. (Function of alternative splicing), which you read on Saturday — this one adds the regulatory mechanisms. Question to keep in mind: if splicing is kinetic competition between sites, what does that suggest about a sensible generative model for isoform proportions — independent per-isoform rates, or something structured by shared exons?

extras.summary: Chapter 7 derives backpropagation — first on a scalar toy chain (sin, exp, cos) and then for a deep ReLU network — as a forward pass that stores activations followed by a backward pass that reuses derivatives layer by layer. It then shows why initialisation matters: with zero biases and N(0, σ²) weights, activation and gradient variances scale by ½·D_h·σ² per layer, so He initialisation (σ² = 2/D_h) keeps them stable.
takeaways: Backprop = chain rule computed in reverse order so shared terms are reused; weight gradients are ∂ℓ/∂f_k · h_kᵀ, so they are proportional to the stored activations (Eq. 7.23–7.25).
Going backwards alternates two cheap steps: multiply by Ω_kᵀ, then mask with the ReLU indicator I[f > 0] — efficient in compute but memory-hungry because every activation must be stored.
He init σ² = 2/D_h (forward) or 2/D_h′ (backward), compromise 4/(D_h+D_h′); too small or too large gives vanishing or exploding signals (Fig. 7.7).
pitfalls: Students confuse ∂ℓ/∂f_k (pre-activations) with ∂ℓ/∂h_k (activations) — have them label both in the toy chain of Eq. 7.9 before touching matrices.
The transpose in ∂f/∂h = Ωᵀ looks arbitrary — explain it as 'gradients flow back along the same arrows, so the shapes must flip'; a 2×3 example on the whiteboard settles it.
Why ReLU gives the factor 2 in He init: half the pre-activations are clipped, so E[h²] = σ_f²/2 (Problem 7.14); Xavier/Glorot lacks this factor.
extras.links: Reverse-mode differentiation through a stored computational graph is exactly what makes your flow-matching and CTMC training loops cheap, and the memory cost of storing activations is the same issue adjoint methods (Neural ODEs, on your path) were designed to avoid.

extras.summary: Chapter 10 motivates convolutional layers from three properties of images (high dimension, local correlation, stability under translation) and defines invariance f[t[x]] = f[x] versus equivariance f[t[x]] = t[f[x]]. It builds 1D then 2D convolution (kernel size, stride, padding, dilation, channels, receptive fields), down/upsampling including transposed and 1×1 convolutions, and closes with AlexNet, VGG, YOLO and a segmentation network.
takeaways: A convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with most weights zero and the rest shared (Fig. 10.4) — a strong inductive bias, which is why on MNIST-1D the CNN reaches ~17% test error versus ~40% for a fully connected net that could in principle represent it.
Convolution is translation-equivariant; pooling and downsampling add partial invariance, so classification nets end invariant while segmentation nets stay equivariant.

Shape bookkeeping: C_i × C_o × K × K weights plus C_o biases per layer; receptive fields grow with depth, stride and dilation; 1×1 convolutions change channel counts and act as a per-position fully connected network.
pitfalls: Output-size arithmetic with padding/stride/dilation — give students the formula and have them check it against PyTorch's printed shapes before building anything.
Thinking a 3×3 kernel on an RGB image has 9 weights — it has 3×3×3 per output channel; drawing the kernel as a small cube helps.
Invariance vs equivariance get mixed up — use the classification vs segmentation example of Fig. 10.1 (label stays fixed vs mask moves with the image).
extras.links: Equivariance as an architectural prior is the same idea that runs through the GRL track (Hamilton's book) and E(n)-equivariant GNNs on your path, just with the translation group in place of permutations or rotations.

summary: Standard guidance steers a diffusion model towards a single condition; Jeffrey guidance instead moves a whole marginal p(y) of some feature y = u(x) to a prescribed target p*(y) while keeping p(x|y) fixed, which by Jeffrey's rule gives p*(x) = ρ(u(x)) p(x) with ρ = p*/p. The density ratio ρ is estimated with a classifier separating target from model samples, and its gradient (evaluated at the Tweedie estimate x̂₀) is added to the score late in sampling. Matching Inception-embedding distributions cuts FID substantially on CIFAR-10 and FFHQ, and on CelebA-HQ it rebalances or decorrelates attributes.
takeaways: Jeffrey's rule is the minimal update of a joint that imposes a new marginal (an information projection); ordinary conditioning is the special case where p*(y) is a point mass.

With a deterministic feature map the target is an exponential-style tilt p(x)·ρ(u(x)), so the guidance term is ∇ log ρ(u(x̂₀)) — classifier guidance generalised from one class to a whole distribution.
In practice it relies on approximations: x̂₀ via Tweedie, a classifier-based ratio, a strength λ (λ = 1 is the exact Jeffrey update) and a late-time window δ; decorrelation needed λ > 1.
keyFigure: Fig. 1: overview — where classifier guidance targets a single class, Jeffrey guidance updates p(y) towards a target p*(y) via a correction term added at each diffusion step.
relevance: Jes and Pierre-Alexandre Mattei's guidance line (with Razafindralambo, Sun, Precioso): it gives a principled way to make a pretrained model match a target marginal. For you that could mean nudging a trained isoform generator so a summary statistic — e.g. the distribution of an isoform's usage fraction or of gene totals in a new cell population — matches observed data, without retraining.
brief: Focus on Sec. 2.1 (Jeffrey's rule, Eqs. 2–5) and Sec. 3.1 (the guidance term, Eqs. 12–15); the experiments can be skimmed for the λ/δ trade-off. It connects directly to the flow-matching guidance survey (fmguide) you read yesterday — place it in that taxonomy as a marginal-matching tilt. Question to keep in mind: on a discrete state space like your lattice simplex, the tilt ρ(u(x)) has no gradient — would you apply it as a rate reweighting of the CTMC generator instead (the paper's Eq. 12 hints at the non-differentiable case)?
news: No new papers from Jes or the group this week on arXiv. Worth a glance: 'Binary Discrete Diffusion' (von Rütte, Schölkopf, Hofmann et al.), a CTMC corruption kernel over candidate sets — it's in today's Discover.

extras.summary: Chapter 5 reframes a network as predicting the parameters of a distribution over outputs, and derives every loss from one recipe: choose Pr(y|θ), let the network output θ = f[x,ϕ], minimise the negative log-likelihood. Least squares, binary and softmax cross-entropy, heteroscedastic regression and multi-output losses all fall out of it, and cross-entropy is shown to equal NLL via the KL to the empirical distribution.
takeaways: The four-step recipe (Sec. 5.2): pick a distribution on the output domain, predict its parameters, minimise NLL, and at inference return the full distribution or its mode.

Least squares = Gaussian likelihood with predicted mean; binary cross-entropy = Bernoulli with a sigmoid; multiclass cross-entropy = categorical with a softmax. Predicting σ² too (with a positivity map) gives heteroscedastic regression.
Cross-entropy and NLL are the same objective (Sec. 5.7): minimising KL from the empirical distribution of Dirac deltas leaves exactly the summed log-likelihood.
pitfalls: 'Why log?' — log turns a product of per-sample likelihoods into a sum and doesn't move the argmax; it's also numerically stable.
Thinking the network outputs y rather than θ — draw the pipeline x → f → θ → Pr(y|θ); the prediction ŷ is just the mode of that distribution.
Positivity/constraints on parameters (σ², probabilities) — the network outputs unconstrained numbers, so a link function (square/softplus, sigmoid, softmax) maps them into the valid domain.
extras.links: This is the same likelihood-first view as your NB + multinomial model: gene totals get an NB likelihood and isoform splits a multinomial, i.e. exactly 'choose Pr(y|θ) for the output domain' — a nice concrete example to show students who work with counts.

extras.summary: Chapter 6 covers fitting: gradient descent, local minima and saddle points, SGD with batches and epochs, momentum (incl. Nesterov) and Adam. Adam normalises each coordinate by a running estimate of the squared gradient and adds momentum and bias correction, which makes progress even when the loss is much steeper in one direction than another.
takeaways: SGD uses a fresh random batch each step: cheaper per step, adds noise that helps escape saddle points and poor minima, and is usually run with a decaying learning-rate schedule.
Momentum averages past gradients, smoothing the trajectory and speeding progress along shallow valleys.

Adam (Eqs. 6.15–6.17) = momentum on the gradient and on its square, plus bias correction 1/(1−βᵗ); it moves roughly a fixed step per coordinate, so it is less sensitive to the initial learning rate and balances updates across layers.
pitfalls: Epoch vs iteration vs batch — one iteration = one batch gradient step; one epoch = one pass over all data (Sec. 6.2.1).
Why Adam needs bias correction — m and v start at zero, so early averages are shrunk towards zero; dividing by 1−βᵗ undoes that and its effect fades as t grows.
'Adam always wins' — it's less sensitive to learning rate but still has hyperparameters (α, β, γ, batch size); Sec. 6.5 frames these as things to search over, and students should still tune α.
extras.links: Every model in your work (flow/generator matching, VAEs) is trained this way; the noisy-gradient view also connects to the stochastic objectives in diffusion training, where each step samples data, time and noise — a good example of why SGD's noise is fine.

brief: Starting point for the whole path. Read it as a catalogue: skim the mechanisms (domain changes, localisation signals, NMD, UTR effects) and note two or three examples you'd want to look for in your own isoform data. Tomorrow's papers on proteome expansion and the Tress/Blencowe debate lean on this vocabulary.
relevance: This is the biological reason to model isoform proportions within a gene separately from gene totals, as your NB + multinomial factorisation does. The mechanisms it lists are roughly the consequences IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR annotates (domain loss, signal peptides, disordered regions, NMD sensitivity), so they are the natural way to interpret any isoform shift your generative model or scIso predicts.
summary: A long review that catalogues what alternative splicing does to the proteins it produces. It goes mechanism by mechanism: changes to binding domains and interaction partners, enzymatic activity, subcellular localisation, stability and post-translational modification. It also covers isoforms that are never translated because a premature stop codon sends them to nonsense-mediated decay.
takeaways: Splicing rarely switches a protein fully on or off. More often it adds or removes a short module (a binding motif, a localisation signal, a modification site) that changes how the protein is regulated.
Many alternative exons are short and encode disordered regions, so their effect is easy to miss if you only look at folded domains.
A large share of isoform changes act on the RNA rather than the protein, through decay or changed untranslated regions, so a shift in isoform proportions does not always mean a new protein.
